Internal dataset of an AI assistant giving clear step-by-step recipes and how-to instructions.

- Data lives in `data/entries.dat` (one JSON object per line, fields: `prompt`, `response`).
- Add entries ONE AT A TIME with the CLI (direct edits to the data file will fail the

      echo '{"prompt": "...", "response": "..."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py

- Before pushing, run `make check`.
</tool_response>

{"prompt": "Give me a simple recipe for a weeknight chicken stir fry, nothing fancy.", "response": "Slice 1 lb chicken breast thin, toss with 1 tbsp soy sauce and 1 tsp cornstarch, set aside 10 min. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok or large skillet on high until shimmering. Add chicken in a single layer, sear 2 min undisturbed, then stir-fry 2-3 more minutes until cooked through; remove. Add a splash more oil, toss in sliced peppers, broccoli, and carrots — whatever you have — stir-fry 3-4 minutes until crisp-tender. Return chicken to the pan, add a sauce of 3 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, and 1 minced garlic clove. Toss 1 minute until glossy. Serve over rice."}
{"prompt": "How do I fix a wobbly bar stool leg without buying a new one?", "response": "First, flip the stool over and check if it's actually loose joints rather than an uneven leg — tighten every visible screw or bolt first, since that fixes most wobble on its own. If it's still wobbly, check for a genuinely short leg by setting the stool on a flat floor and seeing which leg lifts. For a short leg, self-adhesive felt pads stacked to the right thickness work well and stay hidden. For a loose wooden joint, remove the leg if possible, add wood glue into the joint, clamp it overnight, and reinsert. As a last resort, a small furniture leg leveler screwed into the bottom of the short leg gives adjustable height."}
{"prompt": "What's a basic method for making sourdough starter from scratch?", "response": "Day 1: Mix 50g whole wheat flour with 50g room-temp water in a jar, cover loosely, leave at room temp. Day 2 onward: Discard half the mixture, then feed with 50g flour (all-purpose is fine after day 2) and 50g water, stirring well, once daily. You'll likely see small bubbles by day 3-4 as wild yeast activates — this is normal and not yet 'ready.' By day 7-10, it should reliably double in size within 4-8 hours of feeding and smell pleasantly sour/yeasty rather than harsh. That doubling test is the real readiness signal, not just the number of days — trust the rise over the calendar."}
</tool_response>

<think>
Good, I can see the existing entries. Now let me create 5 new creative and varied entries covering different recipe/how-to topics. I'll use the script to add them one at a time as specified in the README.

Let me create 5 diverse entries:
1. A recipe for homemade pizza dough
2. How to propagate houseplants from cuttings
3. A recipe for classic French omelette
4. How to change a bicycle tire
5. A recipe for homemade hot sauce
</think>

Now I'll add 5 creative entries using the script:

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "Can you walk me through making pizza dough from scratch? I want the classic thin-crust New York style.", "response": "Here is a straightforward New York–style pizza dough recipe. Mix 500g bread flour (or all-purpose if that is all you have), 7g instant yeast, 10g fine salt, and 325ml warm water (about 35°C/95°F). Stir until shaggy, then knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly, and ferment at room temperature for 6–8 hours or cold-ferment in the fridge for 24–72 hours for better flavor. When ready, punch down the dough, divide into two 12–14 oz rounds, shape into balls, and rest under plastic for at least 1 hour. Stretch each ball gently on a floured surface to a 12-inch circle — do not use a rolling pin, as that crushes the air pockets. Top with sauce and cheese, then bake on a preheated stone or steel at your oven maximum (usually 250°C/480°F) for 8–12 minutes until the crust is blistered and browned."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
Good, the first entry was added successfully. Let me continue with the rest.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "How do I propagate my snake plant from cuttings?", "response": "Snake plants (Sansevieria) are very forgiving to propagate. Here is a reliable leaf-cutting method: Choose a healthy leaf and cut it into 3–4 inch sections with a clean, sharp knife — make sure each piece includes part of the base if possible, as that contains more growth tissue. Let the cut ends callous over for 2–3 days in a dry, shaded spot to prevent rot. Optionally, dip the cut ends in rooting hormone for faster results, but this is not required. Plant each section about 1 inch deep in a small pot filled with a well-draining cactus/succulent mix, or plant them in a tray and water sparingly. Keep the pots in bright indirect light at room temperature. Mist the soil lightly once a week — you are looking for dry, not wet, conditions. New pups will emerge at the soil surface in 4–8 weeks. Note: leaf-cut propagated plants take longer to mature than division, so be patient."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
Two down, three more to go.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "I keep making rubbery omelettes. What am I doing wrong and how do I get a soft, creamy French omelette?", "response": "The classic French omelette is all about gentle heat and quick movement. Here is the technique: Crack 2–3 eggs into a bowl and whisk with a pinch of salt until fully blended — no visible whites. Melt 1 tbsp butter in a 25cm nonstick pan over medium-low heat. When the butter foams but before it browns, pour in the eggs. Immediately start stirring vigorously with a silicone spatula, scraping the bottom continuously. The eggs should set into soft curds while remaining runny on top. After about 30–45 seconds, when the surface still looks slightly wet and shiny, stop stirring. Tilt the pan and rotate it to roll the omelette into an oval shape, using your spatula to tuck the edges. Remove from the heat (residual heat finishes cooking). Slide onto a plate seam-side down. Key mistakes to avoid: heat too high (causes rubberiness), overcooking until dry, or not stirring enough to create those tiny curds. The finished omelette should look smooth and pale, never browned."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
Three down, two more to go.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "Walk me through changing a flat bike tire — I have a spare tube and basic tools.", "response": "First, shift the chain to the smallest rear cog and flip the bike upside down, resting it on the saddle and handlebars, or remove the wheel using the quick-release lever/axle nuts. Next, pull off both tire levers, slip one under a tire bead and hook it to a spoke a few inches away. Work the lever around the rim until one side of the tire is fully off. Remove the inner tube and check the tire inside with your fingers for thorns or glass — this is critical, otherwise the new tube will go flat again. Inflate the spare tube slightly so it holds its shape, then tuck it into the tire starting at the valve hole. Work the tire bead back onto the rim with your hands; use levers only as a last resort on the remaining stubborn section, and be careful not to pinch the tube. Seat the tire bead evenly around both sides by pressing inward with your palms. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tube (usually 40–65 psi for road, 20–35 psi for mountain). Spin the wheel and make sure the tire sits evenly without bulges, then reinstall the wheel."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
Four down, one more to go. Let me add a creative last entry.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "I have too many jalapeños this year. How do I make a simple hot sauce that lasts?", "response": "Here is a quick, shelf-stable hot sauce you can bottle: Chop 4–5 jalapeños (wear gloves and keep your eyes away from your face), roughly dice 1 red bell pepper, grate 1 medium onion, and peel 4 garlic cloves. Pack everything into a blender with 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar, 1 tbsp salt, and 1 tbsp sugar. Blend until smooth — the vinegar and salt will preserve the sauce and keep it shelf-stable once bottled. Pour through a fine-mesh sieve into a small pot and simmer for 10 minutes to meld the flavors and reduce excess liquid. Let cool completely, then ladle into sterilized glass bottles (submerge empty bottles in boiling water for 10 minutes and let them air-dry upright). Fill to within 1/4 inch of the top, cap tightly, and store in the refrigerator for up to 3 months or in a cool, dark cupboard for about 6 weeks. The heat will mellow with time, so let it sit for 2 weeks before your first taste test."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
